overview: A recurring thread this week is that apparent limits on cognitive control depend on context and design. [Large rewards improved task switching but increased interference costs](#p0), which may explain why evidence for a flexibility-stability trade-off has been mixed. [Pre-cue benefits for upcoming distraction](#p1) appeared in blocked designs only when informative cues came first, but appeared reliably when cue types were intermixed. [A visual search study](#p3) found that the dominant display type sets a processing mode that carries over to trials of the other type, which determines whether salient distractors capture attention. On working memory, [a probabilistic inference theory that maps onto a recurrent circuit](#p7) and [a single model trained on five image-memory tasks](#p6) both try to unify behavior and mechanism, the latter showing more false alarms as more images are seen even while sample memory stays robust. Among the standouts, [surprise improved report of an otherwise forgotten target feature](#p4), including when the surprise was a contextual or auditory change. [Serial dependence emerged spontaneously in recurrent networks trained to denoise video](#5

papers.title: Something's gotta give: Reward-induced effort modulation in task-switching reveals a flexibility-stability trade-off
papers.authors: Nathan K. Mathews, Senne Braem, Eliana Vassena et al.
papers.summary: Across two experiments (N = 80 and 87), people did a task-switching paradigm with reward cues, and big rewards made them better at switching tasks (smaller switch costs) but worse at ignoring interference (larger incongruence costs). In the first experiment the same inverse relationship showed up across blocks under reward. It's a neat way to explain why earlier evidence for a flexibility-stability trade-off was mixed: the trade-off may come from how effort shifts when rewards are on the line.
papers.abstract: Everyday behavior requires balancing two control modes: flexibility, for switching between tasks, and stability, for maintaining goals in the face of interference. One influential account posits that these modes trade off, such that increased flexibility comes at the cost of reduced stability. However, empirical support for this trade-off remains equivocal. We propose that it arises from reward-induced effortful control modulations during tasks that require both modes simultaneously. Across two experiments (N = 80 and N = 87), participants completed a task-switching paradigm in which cued reward incentives were manipulated over varying timescales. Large rewards increased flexibility, evinced by reduced task switch costs, but reduced stability, evinced by increased incongruence costs. In Experiment 1, this trade-off also emerged across blocks, with fluctuations in stability and flexibility inversely related under reward. Overall, these findings provide evidence for a reward-driven flexibility-stability trade-off, in which higher incentives promote flexibility at the cost of stability.

papers.title: Mind the cueing design: Order effects mask benefits of congruency pre-cues
papers.authors: Christopher O. Nuño, Máté Gyurkovics, Julie M. Bugg
papers.summary: People often fail to show benefits from pre-cues warning them about upcoming distraction, which has made it look like proactive control has limits. In two pre-registered experiments, the researchers found that the usual between-block design hides the benefit depending on block order. Benefits appeared only if informative cues came first, whereas intermixing informative and uninformative cues within blocks gave reliable benefits regardless of order, and this was replicated in a second experiment. So some of the apparent limits may come from the design rather than from the mind.
papers.abstract: Evidence that individuals proactively adjust cognitive control in response to pre-cues signaling upcoming distraction has been surprisingly sparse, raising questions about the limits of volitional control. The present study tested whether this pattern reflects genuine constraints in proactive control engagement or methodological limitations of standard pre-cueing designs. Across two pre-registered experiments, we examined the role of cueing order (i.e., whether participants started with informative or uninformative pre-cue blocks) in the commonly used between-block design and evaluated an alternative within-block design in which informative and uninformative pre-cues were randomly intermixed. In Experiment 1, the standard approach of collapsing cueing order conditions yielded null pre-cue benefits for the between-block comparison, mirroring what is often observed in the literature. However, when considering cueing order, benefits emerged when informative cues were encountered first (cued-first group) but not when they appeared second (uncued-first group). In contrast, the within-block comparison produced reliable pre-cue benefits regardless of cueing order. Experiment 2 replicated the within-block pre-cue benefit using a fully intermixed design without the cueing order manipulation. Together, these findings indicate that sparse evidence for pre-cue benefits may partly reflect design-related constraints rather than limits in proactive control. Why pre-cue benefits depend on cueing order remains an open question, but the present findings reveal that the intermixed cueing design offers a more sensitive and reliable method for detecting cue-based control adjustments-with important implications for prominent theories of cognitive control.

papers.title: Uncovering internal sensory evidence reveals the nature of confidence computation in multi-alternative perceptual decision making.
papers.authors: Kai Xue, Medha Shekhar, Dobromir Rahnev
papers.summary: Modeling confidence in tasks with many choices is hard because nobody knew how stimuli turn into internal evidence in those cases. Here, using numerosity tasks with two, three and five choices, the researchers show a simple two-parameter equation can describe that internal evidence across up to 12 conditions. With that in hand, they tested six theories of confidence and found support for the one where confidence reflects the raw evidence difference between the top two alternatives.
papers.abstract: A central goal of perceptual decision making is to determine the computations underlying choice and confidence in complex, multi-alternative tasks. However, revealing these computations requires knowledge of the internal sensory evidence upon which the computations operate. Unfortunately, unlike for two-choice tasks, there is no established method in multi-alternative tasks to determine how stimuli are transformed into internal sensory evidence. Here we address this critical gap by developing a novel modeling paradigm that reveals how the brain transforms external stimuli into internal sensory evidence during multi-alternative decision making in the context of numerosity tasks. Across three experiments that feature two-, three-, and five-choice conditions, we show that the internal sensory evidence in our numerosity task can be described with a simple, two-parameter equation that fits data for up to 12 conditions. Critically, the ability to model the internal sensory evidence allowed us to test six theories of confidence computation. Our results support a model where confidence reflects the raw evidence difference between the top two alternatives. These results establish a new numerosity paradigm in which a two-parameter equation can be used to determine the internal sensory evidence for a potentially unlimited number of multi-alternative conditions and reveal the confidence computation in multi-alternative tasks. papers.title: Switching between singleton-detection and feature-search mode in visual search.
papers.authors: Dock H. Duncan, Jan Theeuwes
papers.summary: In visual search, a long-running debate asks whether attention capture is driven by top-down search settings or by the search process itself. Here, the dominant display type in an experiment (heterogeneous or homogeneous) pushed people toward feature search or singleton detection, and that mode persisted even on the occasional trials with the other display type. When heterogeneous displays dominated, search was slow and salient distractors didn't capture attention, even on homogeneous trials. When homogeneous displays dominated, search was faster and capture occurred across trial types, suggesting capture depends on the processing mode set by context rather than just the current display.
papers.abstract: There has long been a debate in visual search about whether attentional capture is determined by top-down search settings or by the structure of the search process itself. We addressed this issue in two experiments in which participants searched for the same target shape, while the dominant trial context biased the search mode toward either feature search or singleton detection. To assess whether multiple items were processed in parallel or more serially, we also included a two-target compatibility manipulation, in which some trials contained two targets associated with either compatible or incompatible responses. In Experiment 1, most trials (10/11) contained heterogeneous displays, which required participants to adopt the feature-search mode to locate the target. In Experiment 2, most trials contained homogeneous displays, allowing participants to rely on singleton detection to locate the target. On a minority of trials (1/11), the opposite display type was presented, allowing us to test whether the dominant search strategy would persist across changing displays. The results showed strong contextual persistence. When heterogeneous displays predominated, search was slow, Target-Target Compatibility effects were absent, and salient distractors failed to capture attention, even on homogeneous display trials in which singleton-detection mode could in principle be used. When homogeneous displays predominated, allowing singleton-detection mode to be adopted, search was faster, compatibility effects emerged, and salient distractors captured attention across trial types. These findings suggest that attentional capture depends on the mode of processing induced by the predominant display context, rather than on the properties of the current display alone. papers.title: Surprise Resets the Mind: An Adaptive Online Reset in Working Memory Selection
papers.authors: Jiahan Yu, Jiewei Zheng, Yingtao Fu et al.
papers.summary: Using the attribute-amnesia paradigm, where people attend to and use a target feature but usually can't report it, the researchers introduced a surprise (an expectation violation) on the critical trial. Across six experiments with 250 students, surprise reliably improved report of that feature, even when the violation was a broader contextual or auditory change rather than something about the target. That makes it hard to chalk up to simply paying more visual attention to the target, and suggests surprise triggers a quick readjustment of what gets selected into working memory.
papers.abstract: Human cognition rapidly adapts to unexpected events in dynamic environments, but it remains unclear whether expectation violations rapidly influence the selection of attended information into working memory. Using the attribute-amnesia paradigm, we introduced expectation violations during the surprise trial to test whether unexpected changes improve reporting of a target feature that had been attended and used but was normally not reported. Across six experiments (total N = 250 college students, aged 17–27 years; 149 females), expectation violations reliably improved surprise-trial report of this feature, indicating greater availability in working memory. This effect occurred not only when the violation concerned the target, but also when it involved broader contextual or auditory changes, suggesting that the effect cannot be characterized simply as enhanced visual attention to the target. These findings suggest that expectation violations trigger a rapid, flexible adjustment of working-memory selection, highlighting its role in dynamically managing information under uncertainty.

papers.title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness
papers.authors: Hiroshi Higashi, Keigo Sugihara, Yuichi Tanaka
papers.summary: Why would vision carry information over from the recent past, producing serial dependence? The researchers trained recurrent autoencoders to reconstruct noisy natural videos, with no goal related to perceptual history, and models using memory did better than memory-free ones, especially as noise rose. Tested with Gabors and dots, the models spontaneously showed attractive biases toward previous orientations and locations that matched human data, once a response-autocorrelation confound was controlled. The suggestion is that serial dependence may be a byproduct of denoising.
papers.abstract: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.

papers.title: Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
papers.authors: Mranmay Shetty, Gabriel Kreiman
papers.summary: The researchers built one working-memory model for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. A single trained model handles five tasks, such as remembering a sample while other images appear, categorizing distractors, and judging whether an image is new, guided by cues about which response is needed. The model showed little effect of delay on sample memory, but more false alarms as more images were seen, and accuracy declined with the number of questions asked, even while sample memory stayed robust.
papers.abstract: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

papers.title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
papers.authors: Dongyu Gong, Mario Belledonne, Ilker Yildirim
papers.summary: Working memory research has split into debates over slots versus resources, how attention helps, and persistent versus activity-silent firing. MemGP is a theory that treats working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a finite set of inducing points as the shared resource. In simulations it reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attention benefits and inter-item attraction and repulsion, and it maps analytically onto a recurrent circuit with center-surround connectivity and a mix of persistent activity and synaptic weights. The appeal is that one inference objective covers behavior and neural data together.
papers.abstract: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.

papers.title: Memorable Decision Cues are More Associable With Value
papers.authors: David Halpern, Christopher Sanjeev Iyer, Akram Bakkour et al.
papers.summary: Across five pre-registered experiments, the researchers asked whether how memorable a cue image is affects value-based choice. Memorable images weren't chosen more often, but they led to more accurate retrieval of associated values and more value-sensitive choices, which an exemplar model explains as distinctive cues suffering less interference from competing memories. The model's predictions held: memorability biased choices toward the memorable option when both were high value and away from it when both were low, and the pattern also appeared with common foods.
papers.abstract: When making decisions, we must use the sensory cues available at the moment of choice to predict the values of our options. Yet little is known about how properties of these cues affect the choice process, particularly our ability to retrieve decision-relevant memories. Here, we test whether and how image memorability, the population likelihood of recognizing a particular image, influences memory-guided decisions. Across five pre-registered experiments, memorable cue images were not chosen more overall; instead, they predicted more accurate retrieval of associated values and more value-sensitive choices. We account for this pattern of behavior with a formal exemplar model in which distinctive cues suffer less interference from competing memories during retrieval of associated values. The model predicts, and our data confirm, two interactions: choices are more sensitive to value differences between memorable options, and a difference in memorability biases choices toward the more memorable option when both are high in value, but away from it when both are low. Finally, we find that the same pattern held for choices between common foods, suggesting that shared associative memory processes are recruited for choices involving both novel and highly familiar options. Together, our results suggest that more memorable cues are more associable with value, and provide a process-level account for how memorability influences downstream decisions.

papers.title: The Metacognitive Underpinnings of Offloading Decisions
papers.authors: Janet Metcalfe, Matti Vuorre, Dillon H Murphy et al.
papers.summary: In five experiments, people answered general-knowledge questions, rated their confidence, then chose whether to keep their answer or have the computer supply the correct one. Confidence drove offloading, with high confidence meaning no offloading and low confidence meaning offloading, even when questions were chosen so that confidence was misleading. People also barely responded to the points at stake, even when the points-maximizing choice was to offload everything. So metacognitive feelings steer offloading even when they're wrong or irrelevant.
papers.abstract: In five experiments, we investigated how people's metacognitive assessments influence their decisions about whether to rely on their own answers to questions or to obtain the answers from an external source (i.e., to offload). Participants provided answers to general information questions, rated their confidence, and then decided whether to stick with their answer or be given the correct answer by the computer. To examine how metacognitive accuracy impacts offloading, experiment 2-5 included condition which produced good resolution (using easy and difficult questions), and condition that produced poor resolution (using questions people typically think they know the answers to, but don’t). The value of offloading was also varied across experiments via the assignment of differing numbers of “points” for sticking or offloading. In all experiments, participants were told to maximize the number of points earned, allowing us to investigate whether people optimize offloading decisions. Across all five experiments, participants' confidence in their answers predicted whether they would offload or not: when confidence was high, they did not offload; when it was low, they offloaded. They did this even when their metacognition was faulty. Further, participants were relatively insensitive to the value of the options, even in a condition in which the rational choice to maximize points was to offload everything and ignore metacognition entirely. These findings indicate that, even when metacognitive evaluations are either wrong or irrelevant (rather than being correct and germane), people's offloading choices are strongly influenced by their metacognition.

papers.title: A learning account of cognitive control in word production: A path to new insights into the domain generality of control
papers.authors: Shanhua Hu, Tom Verguts, Nazbanou Nozari
papers.summary: Learning-based models explain how similar context words interfere with word production, but they haven't covered other kinds of interference, like a prepotent distractor. This paper proposes CoCo-PaLM, a learning-based model of interference and control in word production. It captures the previously modeled effects and also predicts sequential effects of control and transfer of control between language and non-linguistic systems. The hope is that it gives a framework for separating domain-general control from how it's implemented in specific domains.
papers.abstract: Various computational models have been proposed to explain interference and its resolution in word production. Of these, incremental learning models provide an elegant explanation of the interfering effects of the similarity between a target word and its context. However, such models have not been extended to explain how the production system deals with other kinds of interference, such as the presence of a prepotent distractor. It thus remains unclear whether incremental learning can furnish a general mechanism for explaining interference and its resolution in word production. This paper proposes the Cognitive Control, Production, and Learning Model (CoCo-PaLM), a comprehensive learning-based model of interference and control in word production. In addition to capturing the previously modeled effects, CoCo-PaLM predicts sequential effects of control, as well as effects involving the transfer of control between the language system and non-linguistic systems. More broadly, the model establishes learning as a computational principle for explaining interference and control and offers a framework for dissociating the neural domain-generality of control from its implementation in specific domains.

papers.title: Long-term formation and offline evolution of conceptual knowledge
papers.authors: Sergi Blanco-Cuaresma, Thomas Peter Reber, Simon Ruch
papers.summary: Do people store concepts as collections of examples or as abstract prototypes, and does abstraction happen offline during rest and sleep? The researchers fit cognitive models to behavioral data from two longitudinal concept-learning studies. Prototype models beat exemplar models from the earliest assessment, and their advantage grew across the offline intervals between sessions. This increase showed up when learning relied on few examples and required separating relevant from irrelevant features in complex, naturalistic stimuli.
papers.abstract: Conceptual knowledge allows us to make sense of new events and helps guide decisions in novel situations. But how conceptual knowledge is acquired and represented is still poorly understood. One view holds that humans merely memorize a collection of specific examples to represent a concept. An alternative view proposes that humans gradually integrate past experiences into abstract prototypes to represent concepts. Importantly, the process of integration and abstraction has been theorized to occur offline - especially during rest and sleep. But direct evidence for an offline integration is scarce. By fitting cognitive models of concept learning to behavioral data from two longitudinal concept learning studies, we find that prototype models explain behavior better than exemplar models from the earliest assessment, and that this advantage increases further across offline intervals between experimental sessions. We further show that these offline increases in prototype dominance are observed when concept learning builds on few examples and requires distinguishing relevant from irrelevant features in perceptually complex, naturalistic stimuli. These findings provide novel insights into how humans distill unique experiences into abstract generalizable knowledge about the world.

papers.title: Children spontaneously compute scalar implicatures
papers.authors: Ebru Evcen, David Barner
papers.summary: Many studies say children fail to compute scalar implicatures, for instance accepting 'some of the horses jumped' when all did. The researchers argue that's partly because those tasks hand children scenarios they wouldn't have imagined. When preschoolers first acted out their own interpretation by coloring pictures and then judged a puppet's action, they almost never colored both disjuncts for 'or' and rarely colored all four objects for 'some'. Afterward they computed implicatures in an adult-like way, more often than children in the standard judgment-only condition.
papers.abstract: A large developmental literature finds that children often fail to compute scalar implicatures, accepting underinformative descriptions such as, “Some of the horses jumped” when all of them did, or, “The bear took a cup or a plate” when he took both. Here, we argue that past studies find such failures because they do not evaluate children’s spontaneous interpretation of utterances, but instead ask how they interpret language when provided proffered “worlds” that children would not consider otherwise. We show that when children are allowed the chance to act upon their own spontaneous interpretation of utterances, they compute scalar implicatures in an adult-like fashion. Specifically, we tested children in two conditions: a standard Truth Value Judgment (TVJ) condition, similar to past studies, and a novel, two-phase Act-Out+TVJ condition in which children first acted on the utterance by coloring pictures before judging a puppet's action. In the act-out task children almost never colored both disjuncts after hearing “or” (Experiment 1) and rarely colored all four objects after hearing “some” (Experiment 2). More importantly, after acting out these interpretations, children computed scalar implicatures in an adult-like fashion, and significantly more often than children in the TVJ-only condition. These findings suggest that preschoolers spontaneously access relevant alternative utterances and compute scalar implicatures when allowed to generate their own interpretations before evaluating experimenter-provided worlds, and that previous studies underestimate this ability by artificially proffering irrelevant worlds.

papers.title: The Dual Nature of Syntactic Node Count: Facilitating and Inhibiting Sentence Comprehension
papers.authors: Kohei Kajikawa, Shinnosuke Isono
papers.summary: Node Count, the number of syntactic nodes built at each word, is used in neurolinguistics as a measure of structure-building effort, yet several studies find it correlates negatively with reading times. The researchers tested whether it instead indexes structure-mediated predictability by relating it to pointwise mutual information and to reading times in three large naturalistic English datasets, across three grammar formalisms. Variants based on integrative parsing steps showed facilitation in immediate regions and a delayed slowdown in spillover regions, and the facilitation explained reading-time variance beyond GPT-2 surprisal. That suggests brain-activity correlations with Node Count need careful interpretation.
papers.abstract: Neurolinguistic research on syntactic processing has used Node Count, the number of syntactic nodes assumed to be built at each word, to investigate how structure-building effort affects brain activity. However, several recent studies cast doubt on the presumed link between Node Count and processing effort; they observe negative correlations between Node Count and reading times. These facilitatory effects raise an alternative hypothesis: rather than reflecting structure-building effort, Node Count may index structure-mediated predictability. To test this hypothesis, we first relate Node Count to an information-theoretic measure of contextual support, the pointwise mutual information (PMI) between a word and its context. We then evaluate the relationship between Node Count and reading times from three large-scale naturalistic English datasets. For these analyses, we derive Node Count under three grammar formalisms (phrase-structure grammar, dependency grammar, and combinatory categorial grammar) and multiple parsing strategies. Variants whose count reflects integrative parsing steps correlate positively with PMI and show a dual behavioral profile: robust facilitation in immediate regions, consistent with structure-mediated predictability, and a delayed slowdown in spillover regions, most consistent with the cost of contextual semantic integration. The facilitatory effect explains reading-time variance beyond GPT-2 surprisal, indicating that Node Count has unique psycholinguistic value as an index of human prediction. These results highlight the role of structural representations in human language processing and underscore the need for a careful interpretation of the observed correlations between Node Count and brain activity in neurolinguistic studies.

papers.title: Remembering the unfolding of emotional events: Reduced temporal compression for negative but not positive events
papers.authors: Charline Colson, Arnaud D'Argembeau
papers.summary: Remembering an event usually takes less time than the event itself, and earlier work found this compression is weaker for negative events. Here, people watched positive, negative and neutral videos, mentally replayed them, then described and rated their memories. Negative events again showed less compression and longer, more detailed narratives, while positive events looked like neutral ones on those objective measures. Both positive and negative memories were rated as more detailed, dynamic and easier to recall, so positive emotion seems to change how remembering feels without changing how the event's unfolding is represented.
papers.abstract: The time required to remember an event is typically shorter than the actual duration of the past episode. Recent research has shown that this temporal compression is less pronounced for negative than for neutral events, suggesting enhanced preservation of event unfolding. The present study examined whether this effect extends to positive events. Participants watched positive, negative, and neutral videos and then mentally replayed them before verbally describing and subjectively evaluating their memories. Replicating previous findings, negative events were replayed with less temporal compression than neutral events and were described with longer and more episodically detailed narratives. In contrast, positive events did not differ from neutral events on any of these objective measures, although both negative and positive memories were rated as more detailed, more dynamic, and less difficult to recall than neutral ones. These findings suggest a valence asymmetry in the representation of event unfolding: negative emotion preserves more of an event’s temporal course, whereas positive emotion enhances the subjective experience of remembering without enriching the objective representation of how the event unfolded.

papers.title: Prospective Gains Introduced During Retrieval Enhance Recognition Sensitivity
papers.authors: Gizem Filiz, Ian Dobbins
papers.summary: Incentives are known to boost memory when they're offered at encoding, but this team tested what happens when the prospect of gains or losses is introduced at retrieval, across 238 people and three feedback conditions. Prospective gains improved recognition sensitivity by raising hit rates, while losses helped only a little and only under one feedback type, by lowering false alarms. Drift diffusion modeling suggested gains improved the recovery of memory evidence for old items, whereas both gains and losses made people more cautious in responding.
papers.abstract: Providing incentives encoding reliably enhances subsequent memory, yet their effects at retrieval remain unclear. We contrasted prospective Gains, Losses, and Neutral conditions at retrieval to examine their effects, and we additionally manipulated the nature of feedback provided across three groups (Ntotal = 238). Under Score Change feedback, participants received point increases for accurate responses under Gain trials and point decreases for errors under Loss trials; no other outcomes affected totals. Under Score Change plus Accuracy feedback, participants additionally received trial-by-trial recognition accuracy feedback for all responses, regardless of whether they affected point totals. These groups were contrasted with a No Feedback control group. Across groups, prospective Gains reliably increased recognition sensitivity relative to Neutral prospects by selectively increasing hit rates. Loss prospects produced a mild sensitivity improvement, eliciting a lowered false alarm rate relative to Neutral prospects but only for the Score Change feedback group. Drift diffusion modeling revealed that regardless of feedback group, prospective Gains selectively increased drift rates for old items relative to Neutral and Loss prospects, indicating enhanced recovery of mnemonic evidence. In contrast, prospective Gains and Losses increased boundary separation relative to Neutral trials, reflecting greater response caution. Thus, at retrieval, prospective Gains and Losses have dissociable effects on memory, and the former increase sensitivity providing an adaptive means of prioritizing accurate memory when retrieval yields rewards.

papers.title: Counting on Suppression: Does Learning to Ignore Distractors Depend on Executive Resources? A Registered Report
papers.authors: Francisco Garre-Frutos, Miguel A. Vadillo, David Shanks et al.
papers.summary: Learning to ignore a location where a salient distractor often appears is usually considered automatic, but earlier dual-task tests may not have really taxed executive resources during learning. This registered report plans to have one group count targets with a particular line orientation during the search task itself, and compare their suppression effect with a no-load group. If suppression shrinks or disappears under load, it would mean earlier null results came from secondary tasks that left executive resources free.
papers.abstract: Observers can learn to suppress the locations where salient distractors tend to appear, so that distractors at these locations are less likely to capture attention. This learned distractor suppression is thought to depend on an automatic mechanism that does not require working memory resources. However, previous dual-task studies in this literature have often asked participants to retain or manipulate information that was tested after search, which does not necessarily engage executive processes during learning. In the present study, we will test more directly whether learning to suppress a distractor location depends on executive resources. To do so, participants will perform an additional singleton task while counting the targets that contain a given line orientation, a concurrent executive task integrated into the search itself. We will compare this load group with a no-load control group that will perform the same task without the concurrent task. We hypothesise that the suppression effect will be smaller in the load group than in the control group (H1). Moreover, if this form of learning requires executive resources, the suppression effect could be absent in the load group (H2). The results will show whether learned distractor suppression is independent of executive resources, or whether previous null results reflect secondary tasks that left these resources available during search.

papers.title: Task effects on predictive eye-movements
papers.authors: Jude Thomas Wells Singleton, Hannah Treadway, Claire Kuntz et al.
papers.summary: Two visual-world eye-tracking studies asked whether listeners' predictions from a verb, like looking toward something edible after hearing "eat", change when the verb's relevance to the task changes. Implicit shifts in relevance did little, so associative prediction looks largely automatic. Telling people explicitly to predict, though, boosted prediction and made it start earlier regardless of how predictive the verb was, possibly by enhancing predictive visual search.
papers.abstract: Research on predictive processing has shown that listeners anticipate upcoming linguistic information using linguistic cues, such as verb meaning. Beyond information in the input, listeners’ prediction can also be influenced by top-down control, such as goals and strategies developed in response to a given task. However, it is unclear to what extent evaluations of task relevance modulate top-down control of prediction. We present evidence from two eye-tracking studies in the Visual World Paradigm that associative predictions are largely automatic and not influenced by implicit shifts in the task relevance of a predictive verb. However, when a predictive verb’s task relevance is made explicit in the form of an instruction to predict, prediction is upregulated and initiated earlier irrespective of the verb’s predictiveness, likely due to an enhancement of predictive visual search. Task relevance is thus modulatory for associative prediction when it is specified for listeners.

papers.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Cognitive Control at Short and Long Timescales
papers.authors: Su Wang, Jacob Sellers, Han Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Congruency sequence effects (control adjusting after a recent conflict) and list-wide proportion congruency effects (control adjusting to how often conflict occurs in a block) both reflect cognitive control, but it's been unclear whether they share mechanisms. Using a forced-response paradigm with a computational model, the researchers separated the timing of habitual and goal-directed processing from how likely each was to drive behavior. Both kinds of conflict sped up goal-directed processing, and in the Simon task only, made people more likely to inhibit the habitual response. The block-level effect also remained after accounting for the previous trial, so it isn't just accumulated trial-to-trial effects.
papers.abstract: Response-conflict tasks, such as the Simon and flanker tasks, are widely used to study how individuals exert cognitive control to override prepotent automatic responses (habits) in favor of goal-directed actions (goals). As task demands vary—from local, trial-by-trial interference to global changes in conflict frequency—control parameters may need to be adjusted to maintain task performance. Such cognitive control adaptations can be examined through congruency sequence effects (CSE, the congruency effect is reduced following an incongruent trial compared to a congruent trial) and list-wide proportional congruency effects (LWPCE, the congruency effect is reduced in mostly incongruent compared to mostly congruent blocks). Although both effects involve adjustments in control, it remains unclear whether these adjustments reflect similar or different mechanisms. Here, we used a “forced-response” paradigm combined with a computational model to understand the temporal dynamics of cognitive control that contribute to CSE and LWPCE. This approach allowed us to decompose cognitive control into the latencies of habitual and goal-directed processing and the probabilities with which these processes are expressed as overt behavior. We found that both recent conflict (driving the CSE) and frequent conflict within a block (driving the LWPCE) accelerated goal-directed processing and—in the Simon task only—increased the likelihood of inhibiting the habitual output; the LWPCE persisted after accounting for previous-trial congruency and thus could not be fully reduced to an accumulation of the CSE. These findings indicate that cognitive control adaptations share a common computational signature when regulating conflicts at both short and long timescales.

papers.title: Partially shared representational space for vision and language across objects, scenes, and visual events
papers.authors: Zou, Q., Jozwik, K.
papers.summary: Across three fMRI datasets moving from objects to scenes to dynamic events, the team compared how well vision DNNs, language model embeddings, and human similarity judgments (of images and of their descriptions) predict visual cortex responses, using RSA and variance partitioning. Vision and language converged more in human behavior than in models, and a shared cross-modal component grew along the visual hierarchy and dominated high-level cortex. Language models added the most unique information in face- and body-selective regions, suggesting vision and language share part of a representational space, especially for social information about people and their actions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) and behavioural similarity judgements of visual stimuli predict neural responses in visual cortex. Recent work shows that large language model (LLM) embeddings and similarity judgements of language descriptions also predict visual brain activity. These predictors were examined separately across modalities (vision vs language) and types (models vs human behaviour). It remains unclear to what extent these predictors explain shared or unique aspects of visual brain responses, how these contributions vary along the visual hierarchy and category-selective regions, and whether vision-language convergence depends on the stimulus type. We used three fMRI datasets progressing toward naturalistic visual experience, from objects (THINGS) to scenes (NSD) to dynamic events (BMD). For each dataset, we collected similarity judgements of visual stimuli and of their language descriptions from human participants (N = 21-35), extracted vision DNN features and LLM embeddings, and related similarity judgements and model representations to visual brain responses using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and variance partitioning. Vision-language convergence was higher within behaviour than within models. From objects to dynamic events, LLM alignment with vision-based similarity judgements increased, whereas vision DNN alignment remained stable. A shared, predominantly cross-modal component increased along the visual hierarchy and dominated explained variance in high-level visual cortex. LLMs made their largest unique contributions in face- and body-selective regions (FFA and EBA), where shared representations of vision- and language-based human similarity judgements also explained variance beyond the models. In summary, we find a partially shared representational space for vision and language in high-level visual cortex, most clearly in regions representing social information related to people and their actions. As each predictor retained unique variance, combining computational models and human behaviour across vision and language may offer a more comprehensive account of high-level visual representations.

papers.title: Visual capture of tactile motion: Evidence from a novel mirror box illusion
papers.authors: Anupama Nair, Stephanie Dietz, Jared Medina
papers.summary: Across four experiments, watching a moving stroke across a hand changed where people felt a simultaneous touch moving on their hidden hand, pulling the perceived direction about halfway toward the visual one. The illusion didn't depend on feeling ownership of the seen hand. Changing hand posture showed that the brain draws on both skin-based and external spatial reference frames when constructing the percept of tactile motion, which extends visual capture from where a touch is to its trajectory.
papers.abstract: To localize touch, the brain must integrate information from representations of the skin's surface (a somatotopic reference frame) with representations of the surrounding environment (an external reference frame). While vision robustly captures the perceived location of static touches, resolving crossmodal spatial conflicts for continuous, moving stimuli remains poorly understood. Across four experiments, we demonstrate a novel visual-tactile illusion: viewing a moving stroke across the hand substantially alters the perceived trajectory of a simultaneous tactile stroke on a hidden hand, shifting the percept roughly halfway toward the direction of the visual stroke. This visual capture of tactile motion occurs independently of top-down body ownership. By systematically manipulating hand posture, we found that both somatotopic and external reference frames contribute to the perceived direction of tactile motion. Rather than defaulting to a single coordinate system, the brain combines information from both representations to construct a conscious percept of tactile motion. These results extend visual capture from the location of a touch to its trajectory, and suggest that accounts built on brief, punctate stimuli may need to accommodate both continuous tactile motion and contributions from multiple spatial reference frames.

papers.title: Social relevance reshapes memory encoding and promotes false memories across sensory modalities
papers.authors: Huan Zhang, Xiquan Qin, Hejun Liu et al.
papers.summary: Using a social version of the DRM false-memory task with fNIRS, researchers varied whether words were relevant to the participant, to a partner, or to neither, and whether they were seen or heard. Partner-relevant words led to more false memories than irrelevant ones, even without any misleading information. Frontal and temporal activity during encoding predicted later false memories, while temporoparietal activity seemed to reflect social orienting instead, hinting that social cues can bias encoding and set the stage for memory errors.
papers.abstract: Memory is shaped not only by the information itself but also by its social relevance. The present study investigated whether, in the absence of misleading information, social relevance can increase false memory by altering encoding processes, and whether this effect depends on sensory modality. Using a social DRM paradigm combined with fNIRS, we manipulated item relevance (self-relevant, partner-relevant, irrelevant) and encoding modality (visual, auditory). Behavioral results showed that partner-relevant (vs. irrelevant) items elicited more false memories, indicating that social relevance can enhance false memory even in the absence of explicit misinformation. Neural findings revealed that socially relevant encoding elicited activity within frontal, temporal, and temporoparietal regions, consistent with the notion that social relevance may be linked to spontaneous monitoring processes. Further analyses indicated that frontal and temporal activity predicted subsequent false memory, whereas temporoparietal activity reflected social orienting rather than directly predicting memory distortion. These results suggest that false memory may arise not only from external misinformation but also from encoding biases triggered by social cues. Overall, this study provides new evidence for understanding how social contexts influence false memory and suggests that social relevance may shape subsequent memory performance through attentional and encoding-related processes.

papers.title: Event-general concepts guide semantic generalizations during verb learning cross-linguistically
papers.authors: Sarah Hye-yeon Lee, Anna Papafragou
papers.summary: English and Spanish differ in whether verbs tend to encode manner or path of motion, and the researchers asked how flexible those biases are. Speakers of both languages picked up a new verb bias after a few exposures and applied it to new verbs in the same class, for both spontaneous and caused motion. They also carried the bias across classes, from spontaneous to caused motion and vice versa. That suggests these biases are flexible, higher-level generalizations built on concepts that cut across event types.
papers.abstract: Languages vary in how they map the conceptual components of events onto verbs. For example, some languages, such as English, often encode the manner of spontaneous motion in verbs (e.g., run), while others, such as Spanish, make greater use of verbs that encode the path of motion (e.g., enter). Such verb lexicalization biases are known to be malleable for spontaneous-motion verbs in English. In the present study, we probed the scope and malleability of such biases cross-linguistically. We found that both English-speaking and Spanish-speaking learners can learn new verb lexicalization biases from a few exposures and extend them to novel verb meanings within the same semantic class - in both previously documented and new domains (spontaneous motion - Experiment 1; caused motion - Experiment 2). Furthermore, speakers of both languages could extend verb biases across semantic classes (from spontaneous motion to caused motion - Experiment 1; and from caused motion to spontaneous motion - Experiment 2). These findings indicate that verb lexicalization biases are flexible higher-order semantic generalizations that draw from conceptual dimensions that cross-cut specific event types and support verb learning across languages.

papers.authors: Lily Zihui Zhu, Andrei Amatuni, Shannon Egan-Dailey et al.

papers.title: Pre-stimulus cortical state predicts behavioral performance differently across distractor-learning contexts
papers.authors: Siyi Chen, Fredrik Allenmark, Hao Yu et al.
papers.summary: This reanalysis of an fMRI visual-search dataset (N = 34) asked whether the brain's global signal just before a trial predicts performance, in two groups who learned to ignore either orientation or color distractors. Same-dimension distractors caused strong interference and recruited attention networks, and spatial learning was stronger there. Pre-stimulus global signal predicted response speed in opposite directions in the two groups, slower in one and faster in the other, even though higher global signal generally went with reduced activity across many networks. So the link between brain state and attention depends on what distractor regularities people have learned.
papers.abstract: Performance during distractor-laden visual search may vary with learned attentional settings and ongoing brain state. We reanalyzed an fMRI visual-search dataset (N = 34) to test whether pre-stimulus global signal (GS), a broad state-sensitive BOLD measure, predicts subsequent performance and cortical responsivity across two distractor-learning groups. Participants searched for an orientation target while ignoring (same-dimension) orientation or (different-dimension) color distractors. The spatially biased, more frequent distractor dimension was orientation in one group and color in the other; so, the groups differed in both spatial regularity and relative exposure to each dimension. Same-dimension distractors produced strong behavioral interference and recruited Dorsal Attention and Salience/Ventral Attention networks, whereas different-dimension distractors produced little interference. Spatial learning was also more robust when regularity applied to the target-relevant same dimension. Pre-stimulus GS predicted response speed in opposite directions across groups: higher GS preceded slower responses in the same-dimension spatial-bias group, but faster responses in the different-dimension spatial-bias group. Pre-stimulus Default-Mode Network activity showed a convergent group-dependent pattern. Higher pre-stimulus GS generally preceded reduced activity in Dorsal Attention, Salience/Ventral Attention, Control, Early Visual, and Default Mode regions. Exploratory analyses suggested that associations between neural attenuation and the GS–performance relationship varied by group, particularly on different-dimension trials. Together, these findings reveal the relationship between pre-stimulus cortical state and subsequent attentional performance to differ across distractor-learning contexts, even though GS-related cortical attenuation is largely context-general.

papers.title: People optimistically search for favorite images.
papers.authors: Didrika S. van de Wouw, Ryan T. McKay, Nicholas Furl
papers.summary: In sequential search problems where you can't go back to rejected options, people tend to sample too few numerical values like prices, which has been tied to overly pessimistic priors. Here, across 10 datasets and five image-based contexts, such as picking the most attractive face, people instead sampled too many options every time. Modeling showed most participants were best fit by a biased prior that expected future options to be better than they really would be, so optimistic and pessimistic priors may explain oversampling and undersampling respectively.
papers.abstract: In many real-world decisions, options appear sequentially, and choosing an option ends the search. These situations are often described as "fiancé problems," since one cannot return to a rejected potential marriage partner if a better option is not found. Mathematically optimal decision makers in such scenarios should use prior knowledge about the distribution of option values, such as their expected value and variability, to decide whether continued search is likely to reveal a better option than the one currently available. Previous work shows that people often sample too few options, relative to optimal benchmarks, when searching through numerical economic values such as prices. Recent computational modeling attributes this undersampling to mis-specified, or biased, prior beliefs, whereby participants expect future options to be lower valued than they should. Here, we tested whether biased prior beliefs might also explain the opposite bias: the tendency to sample too many options in image-based searches, such as choosing the most attractive face. In 10 data sets spanning five image-based choice contexts, we replicated oversampling bias in every data set. We applied computational modeling and, across these image-based tasks, most, but not all, participants were best fit by the biased prior model, which expected future option values to be higher than warranted by optimality. Thus, optimistically and pessimistically biased priors may contribute respectively to over- and undersampling biases. These suboptimal search strategies could manifest in real-world decisions such as shopping, choosing dating partners, or evaluating trustworthy job candidates. papers.title: How do readers interpret ambiguous constituents in novel Chinese compound words?
papers.authors: Cheng-Yu Hsieh, Marco Marelli, Kathleen Rastle
papers.summary: How do readers make sense of novel Chinese compounds when a character has several meanings, like 花 meaning flower or to spend? A computational model and human readers both gave priority to characters with a consistent meaningful function, and these consistent characters served as anchors for working out the appropriate meaning of the ambiguous ones. The results suggest that stored knowledge about how reliably forms map to meanings shapes how new words are understood, and that Chinese writing may be more systematic and learnable than it looks.
papers.abstract: Most Chinese words are compounds comprising multiple constituent characters. Research has shown that compounds are routinely broken down into their constituents during word recognition, but it is unknown how readers deal with characters that have multiple possible meanings (e.g., 花 can mean both flower and to spend, depending on the compound in which it appears) and that are highly prevalent in Chinese. The present study investigated how a computational model (Study 1) and human readers (Study 2) compute the meanings of novel Chinese compounds that contain semantically ambiguous characters. We found that both model and human readers prioritise characters that have a consistent meaningful function when making sense of novel compounds, and a further study revealed that semantically-consistent characters serve as anchors to help readers determine the contextually appropriate meaning for ambiguous characters. These findings suggest that the stored knowledge of the consistency of form–meaning mappings shapes the comprehension of novel words. We conclude by arguing that, despite its apparent ambiguity, the Chinese writing system may be more systematic and learnable than it appears.

papers.title: Strategic control or evolutionary bias? Disentangling responsible remembering from adaptive memory.
papers.authors: Dillon H. Murphy, Bennett L. Schwartz
papers.summary: Two accounts of selective memory, automatic survival-tuned biases (adaptive memory) and strategic goal-directed control (responsible remembering), were tested across three experiments. Survival importance ratings predicted recall whether encoding was incidental or intentional, and accurate survival ratings predicted better than arbitrary ones. When the researchers added a rating of importance for making money, the usual survival advantage still appeared in overall recall, but survival and monetary importance predicted item-level memory about equally. The authors suggest responsible remembering may be a flexible extension of adaptive memory rather than a competitor.
papers.abstract: Memory control processes are selective, favoring information important to the individual. In this article, we explore the mechanisms underlying this selectivity. Adaptive memory views posit that selectivity is driven by automatic, evolutionarily tuned biases (i.e., survival relevant), whereas the responsible remembering framework emphasizes strategic, goal-directed control over encoding. In three experiments, we investigated how these two frameworks interact to guide memory prioritization. In Experiment 1, participants rated words for either survival importance or likeability under incidental or intentional encoding conditions. Importance ratings predicted recall across encoding conditions, suggesting that the prioritization of survival-relevant information occurs automatically during encoding, independent of goal-directed strategies. In Experiment 2, participants studied words paired with either accurate or arbitrarily assigned survival-based importance ratings. Although both types of values predicted recall, accurate survival relevance was the stronger predictor. This suggests that although strategic memory is flexible, it is ultimately optimized for processing inherently meaningful information. In Experiment 3, we introduced a control condition evaluating the importance of words for making money. We replicated the classic survival processing advantage in overall recall; however, both survival and monetary importance ratings similarly predicted item-level memory. This indicates that value-based prioritization can guide encoding outside of survival-specific contexts. Together, these experiments suggest that rather than being competing accounts, responsible remembering may reflect a context-sensitive extension of adaptive memory-one that allows strategic prioritization of information based on shifting modern goals, even when fitness is not directly at stake. papers.title: Reading experience influences constructional preferences.
papers.authors: Michelle Perdomo, Duane G. Watson
papers.summary: People who spent the same amount of time reading but across many text categories showed weaker preferences for expected constructions than people who read fewer categories. Because surprisal and constraint-based accounts don't fully explain this, the authors propose a high-exposure flexibility account, in which diverse reading makes processing of unexpected verb-argument combinations more flexible. Exposure to online frequency distributions of constructions only affected dative verb preferences, not phrasal verb preferences.
papers.abstract: ). Participants who spent an equal amount of time reading many text categories revealed weaker preferences for the expected constructions than participants who read fewer categories of text. Because this result is not fully accounted for by surprisal and constraint-based accounts of language processing, we propose the high-exposure flexibility account: More diverse reading exposure leads to more flexible processing of unexpected verb-argument combinations. We find that distributed reading across a variety of texts leads to weaker constructional biases, suggesting better adaptability to novel constructions. On the other hand, experience with online distribution frequencies of constructions only affected dative verb preferences but not phrasal verb preferences. This work highlights the importance of differentiating types of reading experience and their influences on language processing. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Exploiting the dynamics of gaze to modulate the evaluation of risky prospects
papers.authors: Mike E. Le Pelley, Ben R. Newell
papers.summary: Across two incentivized experiments (217 people), a gaze-contingent prompt nudged where people looked while they judged a sure option against a risky one. When gaze was biased toward the risky option, a sure 100 points matched a 50% chance of 266 points. When it was biased toward the safe option, the match rose to 283 points. Total dwell time didn't explain the effect, which fits sequential sampling models better than 'mere exposure' or 'gaze cascade' accounts, because those models say attended options accumulate evidence faster.
papers.abstract: Two incentivized experiments ( N = 217) examined how visual attention contributes to the construction of risk preference. Using a staircase procedure in which participants’ choices were titrated to an indifference point between a sure and risky prospect, we find that a gaze-contingent prompt procedure can influence participants’ risk appetite. Our findings show that, on average, a sure offer of 100 points would be viewed as equivalent to a 50% chance of 266 points when gaze is biased toward the risky option, versus a 50% chance of 283 points when biased toward the safe option. Further aspects of our results and procedure confirm that participants genuinely evaluated risk and reward values, with the influence of the gaze-contingent prompt superimposed on this unfolding process of preference construction. Together our results reinforce the importance of last-fixations for driving preference and as such appear inconsistent with mechanistic accounts that rely solely on ‘mere exposure’ or ‘gaze cascades’, since such accounts see the relationship between gaze and choice as mediated by differences in total dwell time – which was not a pattern supported by our data. By contrast, the current findings could be accommodated by sequential sampling models that propose faster accumulation of evidence for attended options.

papers.title: Visual stimuli modulate phonological prediction during listening comprehension: Evidence from visual world paradigms
papers.authors: Taohui Li, Xiaodong Xu
papers.summary: Two visual world experiments in Mandarin used the same spoken sentences but showed either pictures or printed characters on screen. Semantic prediction showed up in eye movements with both, but predictive phonological effects appeared only with printed characters. The suggestion is that the visual format changes how easily phonological information can be accessed from the display, so what looks like prediction depends partly on what you're looking at.
papers.abstract: The present study investigated whether visual stimulus type modulates predictive phonological activation during spoken language comprehension. Two highly matched visual world paradigm (VWP) experiments were conducted in Mandarin Chinese, using identical auditory sentences but different visual inputs: pictures in Experiment 1 and printed Chinese characters in Experiment 2. Reliable semantic prediction effects were observed in both experiments. In contrast, predictive phonological effects emerged only with printed words. Cross-experiment comparisons further showed that replacing pictures with printed Chinese characters selectively increased the relative phonological competitor effect, reducing its difference from the semantic competitor effect. These findings indicate that visual format affects how predicted phonological information is expressed in eye movements, possibly by changing the accessibility of phonological representations in the visual display.

papers.title: Attention biases the appearance of rapidly alternating stimuli
papers.authors: Arsiak Nabil Ishaq, Erin Goddard
papers.summary: When two colored frames alternate rapidly in the same spot, attending to one makes it look as if that color was on screen longer. The effect appeared when one frame was more salient and so pulled attention automatically, and it was smaller when people were told to attend to one frame on purpose. This extends attention-changes-appearance findings to stimuli sharing a single location. It may also explain why feature conjunctions can still be perceived at 7.5 Hz, faster than binding limits would predict.
papers.abstract: Attentional selection not only increases behavioural performance and neural information for attended stimuli but, in some instances, induces changes in stimulus appearance. While reported appearance changes have mostly concerned the effects of attending to a particular spatial location, here we report a shift in appearance that occurs when attention is directed to one component of a stimulus rapidly alternating at a single spatial location. Our stimuli included two frames of different colors, which alternated at 3.75 Hz or 7.5 Hz. Participants reported the perceived dominance of one frame’s color in the reference stimulus, by comparison with a target stimulus. We found that when one stimulus frame was more salient than the other, with a greater likelihood of capturing exogenous attention, there was an illusory perception that the frame was physically present for a greater proportion of time. When the frames were matched in salience, a task encouraging participants to endogenously direct their attention to one frame produced a smaller shift in appearance. Our results add to the body of literature demonstrating that attention can change appearance—in this case, altering the appearance of attended versus unattended stimuli that are presented at the same spatial location. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that at the ‘temporal transparent’ alternation rate of 7.5 Hz, where rapidly alternating stimuli are perceived as two translucent surfaces, attentional selection of one surface can account for the apparent paradox that feature conjunctions are perceived at stimulus alternation rates higher than predicted by the temporal limits of feature binding for other stimuli. Significance statement We find when stimuli are composed of rapidly alternating frames, attending to one of the frames can change the appearance of the stimuli. Our results add to the growing body of literature demonstrating that attention can change appearance—in this case, for attended versus unattended stimuli that are presented at the same spatial location. Our results also demonstrate that when stimuli alternate at ‘temporal transparent’ rate of 7.5 Hz, perceived as two translucent surfaces, attentional selection of one surface can account for the apparent paradox that feature conjunctions can be perceived, even though each frame is presented only very briefly. Open practices statement The data and materials for all experiments are available in an OSF project ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/5K46J ). This includes trial-level data (MATLAB and CSV files) as well as subject-level data (CSV files), stimulus materials, and MATLAB analysis codes for calculating thresholds. This study was not preregistered.

papers.title: Free recall reveals novel effects of semantic relatedness on recall structure and memory performance
papers.authors: Reut Peled, Roy Luria
papers.summary: Participants studied six-item lists with a semantically related triplet at the start, at the end, or not at all. In serial recall, the triplet boosted accuracy and also helped the unrelated items that followed. In free recall, people tended to put the related chunk last, and doing so went along with better memory for the remaining unrelated items. So semantic relatedness seems to matter at retrieval too, with people saving the sturdier chunk for later.
papers.abstract: Research into human memory has consistently shown that recall is not random but organized by systematic regularities, such as temporal and semantic contiguity. While semantic relationships between items are known to influence memory performance, their impact on the organization of retrieval in unconstrained (free) recall remains less understood. The present study investigated how semantic structure influences both on retrieval organization and memory performance. Across two experiments, participants studied six-item lists containing either a semantic triplet (a "chunk") at the beginning (T1), at the end (T2), or no semantic triplet (NT). Experiment 1 applied a serial recall paradigm to confirm that semantic chunks improve recall accuracy and provide a proactive benefit for subsequent unrelated items. Experiment 2 employed a free recall paradigm to examine whether semantic structures shape retrieval order. Contrary to previous models, which predict that recent or semantically related items are prioritized early in recall, we hypothesized that participants would strategically postpone the retrieval of semantic chunks to later output positions to prioritize items more vulnerable to forgetting. Results demonstrated that while semantic chunks significantly enhanced overall recall performance and provided a proactive benefit, they also fundamentally reshaped retrieval organization: participants were significantly more likely to delay the recall of semantic chunks, shifting them to the end of the output sequence. Importantly, this strategic postponement of the semantic cluster was associated with improved memory for the remaining unrelated items, suggesting that the effects of semantic relatedness on memory performance go beyond the encoding phase by shaping retrieval structure. Open practices statement The experimental task code, raw trial-level data for all experiments, and analysis files are publicly available in the OSF repository ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/62SUQ ). The experiments were not preregistered.

papers.title: When difficulty helps and when it hurts: Target-matching cues yield transient capture while mismatching cues lead to dwelling
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel
papers.summary: Some recent accounts say salient distractors, like abrupt onsets, capture attention more when search is hard and slow. Two visual search experiments tested this with color cues that matched the target, and the pattern came out reversed. Cueing effects were clear in easy, fast search and nearly gone in difficult, slow search. The takeaway is that whether a cue shares features with the target determines how difficulty shapes capture, so the dwelling and accumulation accounts don't carry over to target-matching cues.
papers.abstract: How top-down goals and bottom-up saliency interact over time remains a central debate in visual search. Recent models, such as the Attentional Dwelling Account and the Priority Accumulation Framework, propose that attentional capture by salient, non-matching cues (e.g., abrupt onsets) increases under difficult search conditions (longer reaction times (RTs)), challenging the classical view of transient capture. To test whether this difficulty-dependent modulation generalizes across cue types, we conducted two visual search experiments using target-matching color cues across both feature and singleton search, manipulating task difficulty via color similarity. Across both search types, we observed the inverse of the onset-cue pattern: spatial cueing effects (valid vs. invalid) were pronounced during easy search (short RTs) but virtually eliminated during difficult search (long RTs). These findings indicate that target-matching peripheral cues exert a transient influence, modulating early attentional selection but dissipating before prolonged visual search decisions conclude. Consequently, while attentional dwelling and priority accumulation accounts capture the dynamics of non-matching onset cues, they do not generalize to feature-matching color cues. We conclude that cue type, specifically whether a cue shares defining features with the target, fundamentally determines how task difficulty modulates the time course and magnitude of attentional capture. The data and analysis scripts are available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2CXHE . Open practices statement The following software was used: MATLAB 2022 a (The Mathworks, Natick, MA, USA) with the Psychtoolbox (Brainard, 1997; Kleiner et al., 2007) was used to run the experiment. Statistical analyses were performed using R 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2024) and RStudio 2025.09.1 (Posit team, 2025). The pre-processed data and the analysis code in R are available on the Open Science Framework at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2CXHE . The study’s design and its analysis were not preregistered. The program code used to run the experiments is available on request. Please send an email to dirk.kerzel@unige.ch. Significance statement This paper re-evaluates current priority accumulation and attentional dwelling frameworks. While these models propose that search difficulty increases attentional capture, our findings suggest a more nuanced dynamic: for target-matching color cues, capture appears transient and dissipates as difficulty grows. By showing that the relationship between difficulty and capture depends on cue type, this work highlights important boundary conditions and helps reconcile diverging accounts of attentional control.
