papers.title: Object recognition from dynamic cues: Examining the inversion effect
papers.authors: Niloufar Faridani, Shifa Maqsood, Sophia Robert et al.
papers.summary: To see whether turning things upside down hurts recognition when only motion is available, the researchers turned object videos into kinematograms, where the motion cues drive randomly moving dots. Online participants judged animacy, categorized objects at a subordinate level, and named them, with the displays upright or inverted. Inversion generally impaired recognition, but how much varied by category: animacy judgments showed a small effect for animate items and none for inanimate ones. The authors suggest the variation could reflect objects' natural orientation statistics or the physics of how they move.
papers.abstract: Humans can identify and categorize objects in a dynamic visual scene with remarkable accuracy. To achieve this, our visual system relies not only on static information but also on dynamic cues. Turning a static image upside down hinders recognition. Similar inversion effects have been found in dynamic videos of human action. However, it is unknown whether this inversion effect extends to a broader set of categories when only dynamic cues are available. Here, we used object kinematograms to investigate the inversion effect on object recognition using only dynamic cues. We extracted motion cues from the videos and projected them onto randomly moving dots to create object kinematograms that contain only dynamic information. Participants viewed upright or inverted object kinematograms from four animate and four inanimate categories in an online experiment and completed three tasks: animacy judgment, subordinate-level categorization, and object naming. Overall, inversion impaired object categorization based on motion cues, although the magnitude of the effect varied across categories. For animacy judgment, the animate category showed a small inversion effect, whereas we did not observe a significant inversion effect for the inanimate category. For subordinate categorization and object naming, we observed significant inversion effects in some animate and some inanimate categories. These findings demonstrate that inversion disrupts object recognition even when only dynamic information is available and that the magnitude of this disruption depends on the object category. This variability may reflect differences in the natural orientation statistics of objects or the physical dynamics of their motion.

papers.title: Target detection determined by perceived rather than physical rules: Effect of task-irrelevant Müller–Lyer illusion
papers.authors: Takemasa Yokoyama, Ryoichi Nakashima
papers.summary: With fixation-to-target distance held physically constant, a Müller-Lyer illusion placed between them made the target look either farther or nearer. In a left/right localization task, people were slower when the target looked farther, even though the illusion was irrelevant to the task. So the familiar distance cost seems to follow perceived distance rather than physical distance, which means illusions can change behavior and not just appearance reports.
papers.abstract: Visual perception is not a direct copy of the external environment; contextual information can distort spatial representation, as exemplified by the visual illusion. Illusion research has primarily quantified such distortions through explicit appearance judgments, whereas research on spatial attention and perception has typically manipulated physical fixation-target distance (e.g., target eccentricity) and shown slower responses for more distant targets. These approaches did not determine whether the distance-related performance cost reflected the physical distance itself or the perceived distance encoded in internal spatial representations. Here, we dissociated the physical and perceived distances by holding the physical fixation-target separation constant while selectively distorting the perceived distance with a Müller-Lyer illusion configuration placed between fixation and target during a left/right classification task (i.e., a localization task). Consequently, when the target appeared to be perceptually farther due to the Müller-Lyer illusion, target localizations were delayed compared with when it appeared to be perceptually nearer, despite identical physical distances. These findings demonstrate that the perceived distance rather than the physical distance can determine visual performance. Internal visual representations shaped by illusions can modulate behavior, even without direct task relevance.

papers.title: Distinct Amygdala–Frontopolar and Amygdala–Medial Temporal Pathways Support Temporal Memory for Emotional Events
papers.authors: Jingyi Wang, Joanne E. Stasiak, Neil M. Dundon et al.
papers.summary: In an fMRI study, people saw negative and positive images and later did a surprise test on when each had appeared. More negative images produced more amygdala activity and smaller errors in remembering when they occurred. Stronger amygdala responses predicted more similar activity patterns in the hippocampus, which went with worse temporal memory, but less similar patterns in lateral frontopolar cortex. Amygdala engagement also tracked perirhinal activity, which predicted better item memory and a recency bias. The authors read this as two opposing pathways that can sharpen or blur memory for when emotional events happened.
papers.abstract: Growing evidence suggests that emotion shapes temporal aspects of memory—such as remembering when an event occurred—yet the neural bases of these effects remain unclear. Prior work indicates that temporal context representations in memory are supported by the functions of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and prefrontal regions, including hippocampus, perirhinal cortex, and lateral frontopolar cortex (FPl). These regions have privileged access to amygdala-originated affective signals that may mediate emotional influences on temporal memory. To test whether these candidate pathways shape temporal memory for emotional events, participants encoded trial-unique negative and positive images in the scanner, followed by a surprise temporal memory task. We found that more negative stimuli were associated with greater amygdala activation and lower temporal memory error for when emotional images occurred. Replicating and extending prior work, higher stimulus-evoked multivoxel pattern similarity in the hippocampus and FPl was associated with higher temporal memory error. Notably, greater amygdala responding to emotional images predicted higher between-trial pattern similarity in the hippocampus but lower within- and between-trial similarity in FPl. Amygdala engagement was also correlated with greater perirhinal activation, which in turn predicted stronger item memory and a recency bias in temporal memory estimates. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct—and opposing—modulatory effects of amygdala–FPl and amygdala–MTL pathways on temporal memory, with the potential to sharpen and blur memory for when emotional events occurred.

papers.title: From Novel Combinations to Informative Absence: Structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice in language learning
papers.authors: Yanzhe Zhao
papers.summary: This theoretical and empirical work asks how learners decide that a missing expression is ungrammatical rather than just unobserved. It splits utterance production into structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice, then shows the model can recover which unseen word-construction pairings are allowed in 30 artificial grammars. It also derives how omissions count as evidence depending on context diversity and repetition. Reanalyses of artificial-language experiments (399 participants), child-directed speech corpora, and causative judgments across five languages are used to support the framework.
papers.abstract: Language learners must infer which novel expressions are grammatically licensed and when continued absence is evidence against them. Our generative theory unites these capacities via counterfactual expression opportunities, decomposing utterance generation into structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice. First, shared predictive continuations recover structural permission for unseen word-construction pairings across 30 artificial grammars (mean AUC 0.945 after 120 sentences). Second, under hierarchical uncertainty, we derive a joint evidence law linking omissions to context diversity and within-context repetition, and an exact finite-sample context-refinement inequality. Thus, observing related expressions calibrates expected use to sharpen negative evidence, and higher expected use can drive steeper posterior declines for stronger-permission candidates (reversing initial order after six omissions in a fixed-rate example). Third, we prove that while raw counts confound semantic availability and form selection, scene-level opportunity observations identify both. Empirically, reanalyzing adult and child artificial-language experiments shows meaning-conditioned restriction; judgments of restricted combinations improve held-out production predictions across 399 participants (+0.036 nats/production). Naturalistic child-directed and child speech (11 families, six corpora) shows pervasive source-level usage clustering beyond lexical, number, and dependency-role controls, grounding hierarchical rate uncertainty. Finally, modeling causative judgments across five languages shows that structural compatibility and calibrated usage probabilities draw on distinct distributional, semantic, and discriminative cues. Together, these findings show how the organization and calibration of communicative opportunities govern the evidential value of linguistic absence.

papers.title: Classical visual illusions in vision-language models under an instruction ladder
papers.authors: Eiji Watanabe
papers.summary: Vision-language models often give the 'illusory' answer to classic illusions, and the question here was whether that comes from the image or from knowing the famous figure. The researchers drew 300 new stimuli of 25 illusions, each with a reversed version and a control with the inducing elements removed. They asked two Claude models, with and without thinking, about each image at eight levels of instruction, collecting 460,800 answers. Asked for the physical fact, the models almost never gave the illusion answer, but asked how the picture looks, illusion answers came back even after the truth was stated. For five figures the models also gave illusion answers to the controls, suggesting they were responding to the figure rather than the effect. The stimuli, prompts, and code are released.
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often name the "illusory" answer when shown a classical visual illusion, but it is unclear whether that answer comes from the picture or from knowledge about famous figures. We drew 300 new stimuli of 25 classical illusions in three conditions--the illusion, the illusion with its inducing elements reversed, and a control with the inducing elements removed--and asked about each image at eight rungs of an instruction ladder that runs from a false fact, through a neutral question and an instruction to report the physical truth, to telling the model the name of the illusion and finally the true answer. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, with thinking off and on, gave 460,800 answers. When asked for the physical fact, all four settings almost never gave the illusion answer, and they resolved real 10% differences in the same displays. When asked how the picture looks, the illusion answers returned, and they did not vanish after the true answer was stated. Two measures that cancel position preferences and recognition of the figure suggest that much of this depends on the stimulus: among side answers, Sonnet with thinking chose the illusion side in 85% of cases after being told the truth (95% CI 74--96%), with 16 of the 25 illusions showing a stimulus-driven effect. Yet for five figures--the Fraser spiral, Kanizsa triangle, Pinna--Brelstaff rings, Ouchi pattern and, for Haiku, the rotating snakes--the models gave the illusion answer to the control images as well, which suggests that they answered from the figure rather than from the effect. A false fact was mostly followed on control images but not on illusion images. The stimuli, prompts, all responses and the code are released for testing further models; the Python code that draws the stimuli is parametric and can generate new illusion images for other studies with models or human observers.

papers.title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus
papers.authors: Hiroshi Higashi
papers.summary: Instead of asking how much people differ in judging faces, artworks, photographs, and jokes, this work asks what form the differences take. Three nested models were compared on ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters): same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform allowing reversals, and stimulus-specific offsets. For faces, simple reweighting was enough. For artworks, weights spread along a shared abstract-figurative axis, and 28% of raters fell on the opposite side from the population, though that tail shrank with a different rater sample. The shape of individual differences depends on the domain and the raters.
papers.abstract: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

papers.title: Testing the Speed–Duration Link: Perceptual Equalization of Motion Speed Reduces the Foveal Duration Bias
papers.authors: Hakan Karsilar, Hedderik van Rijn, Sebastiaan Mathot
papers.summary: Peripheral stimuli look slower and shorter than foveal ones, and this study asked whether those are the same underlying effect. After measuring each person's peripheral speed underestimation at about 11° and 22°, the researchers had them compare the durations of foveal and peripheral moving dot patterns, with speeds matched either physically or perceptually. Perceptual speed matching cut the foveal duration bias by about 60%, more so for people who needed larger speed corrections. A bias remained, which points to related but partly distinct mechanisms for speed and duration.
papers.abstract: Visual processing varies systematically with eccentricity: Stimuli in the periphery are perceived as slower, lower in contrast, and shorter in duration compared with foveal stimuli. Whether these asymmetries reflect a single underlying mechanism, such that removing one asymmetry eliminates others, or partly distinct mechanisms remains unknown. We tested this question for perceived motion speed and duration, both underestimated in the periphery, by asking whether perceptually equalizing motion speed across the visual field eliminates or reduces the foveal duration bias. In a two-phase design, each participant's peripheral speed bias was first measured at two eccentricities (approximately 11° and 22°). Participants then compared the durations of foveal and peripheral random dot kinematograms (100–1,600 ms) under physical or perceptual speed equality. The calibration showed robust peripheral speed underestimation at both eccentricities, increasing with distance from fixation. Under physical speed equality, the foveal stimulus was judged to last longer than the peripheral one. Critically, perceptual speed equalization reduced this foveal duration bias by approximately 60%, and this reduction was larger for participants whose calibrated speed correction was larger, consistent with a dose–response relationship. However, a significant residual bias persisted even after perceptual speed equalization. These findings suggest that asymmetries between foveal and peripheral vision do not reflect a single underlying mechanism, but rather reflect a number of partly distinct yet related mechanisms that operate on different features, in this case motion speed and duration.

papers.title: Thinking With AI, Reasoning Without It: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI Weakens Effort Regulation
papers.authors: Dawid Ratajczyk, Agata Dymarska, Adam Matłoka et al.
papers.summary: In a preregistered experiment with 193 participants, some people used ChatGPT on a relational reasoning task and others didn't, with incentives varied separately. Everyone then did a harder task from the same network without AI. ChatGPT helped accuracy at first and made the task feel easier. Afterwards there was some evidence of poorer independent reasoning, and prior users adjusted their effort less to incentives and difficulty. No clear effects appeared on memory. The paper's point is that completing a task with AI is different from building the knowledge and effort regulation needed to do it alone.
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is increasingly used to support learning and problem solving, but it remains unclear how relying on such support affects people's ability to reason independently afterwards. We investigated whether using genAI to solve a complex reasoning task influences subsequent reasoning, memory, and effort when the technology is no longer available. In a preregistered laboratory experiment with a final sample of 193 participants, we used a three-stage relational reasoning task developed for the study, in which participants learned and reasoned about a network of fictional entities and their relationships. During the first stage, participants completed the task either with or without access to ChatGPT, while performance incentives were independently manipulated. All participants then completed a more complex reasoning task based on the same relational network without genAI support, followed by a memory test. GenAI support improved accuracy during the initial task and reduced perceived difficulty. In the subsequent unaided reasoning task, prior genAI use was associated with some evidence of poorer independent reasoning. GenAI use was also associated with weaker adjustment of effort to incentives and task difficulty once the tool was removed. No clear effects were observed on later memory. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of distinguishing successful AI-assisted task completion from the knowledge construction and effort regulation needed to apply the same information independently.

papers.title: Motivated acquiescence: Believing what you want even when you know it’s irrational
papers.authors: Nina Strohminger, David Melnikoff
papers.summary: Theories of wishful thinking usually assume you can only believe what you want if you first convince yourself the belief is rational. Across 13 experiments (ten preregistered, N = 6,613), people endorsed wished-for beliefs while also admitting those beliefs were irrational, a pattern the authors call motivated acquiescence. In a simulated plea-bargaining task it led to negotiation impasses and resisted interventions that normally help people reach agreement. That suggests debiasing methods built on appeals to rationality may not work for these cases.
papers.abstract: Prevailing theories of wishful thinking describe a crucial limit on its powers: To believe what one wants, one must first convince oneself that it is rational to hold this belief. We suggest that this foundational assumption may be incorrect. The results of 13 experiments (ten preregistered; total N = 6,613) suggest that goals can bypass this bottleneck of subjective rationality, leading people to endorse wished-for beliefs while simultaneously acknowledging them to be irrational. We call this phenomenon motivated acquiescence. Motivated acquiescence can have harmful consequences: in a simulated plea-bargaining task, it produced negotiation impasses and was resistant to interventions that reliably promote agreement among non-acquiescers. These findings not only challenge a core assumption about wishful thinking, they have important implications for the efficacy of debiasing interventions that rely on appeals to rationality.

papers.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia
papers.authors: Molly Leachman, Gabriela Muñiz Chams, Lauren K Salig et al.
papers.summary: Children listened to a story while fNIRS (a light-based brain imaging method) recorded their brain activity, and the researchers used language-model surprisal to track how the brain follows phonological, word-level, and syntactic information. Among 140 typically developing children and a matched comparison of 35 children with dyslexia and 35 controls, each level had its own cortical profile. Better reading related to tracking in opposite ways across groups: in dyslexia, higher reading proficiency went with more lexical and syntactic tracking but less phonological tracking, which may mean greater reliance on higher-level information. Syntactic tracking tied to reading in both groups.
papers.abstract: Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

papers.title: Facial expressions assigned to approach are remembered more accurately and evaluated more positively
papers.authors: Arijit De, Kinkini, Jeeviga Yasokaran et al.
papers.summary: Across three online experiments (N = 629), people learned to approach some facial expressions and avoid others, either matching the emotion (approach happy, avoid disgust) or the reverse. Afterwards, memory for expressions was more accurate for whichever category had been assigned to approach, and that category was also rated more positively, even for faces never seen in training. Interestingly, the more positive ratings didn't come with a change in rated arousal.
papers.abstract: Facial expressions guide action, but learned approach–avoidance mappings may in turn shape how expressions are remembered and evaluated. Across three online experiments (total N = 629), participants learned affectively congruent mappings (approach happy faces and avoid disgusted faces) or incongruent mappings (the reverse). Training used looming and receding faces or stationary faces with monetary feedback. Participants subsequently reported previously encountered expressions using an identity-cued wheel constructed from neural-network-generated expression continua and rated facial valence and arousal. Memory accuracy showed a crossover interaction between mapping group and expression category: happy expressions were reported more accurately under congruent than incongruent mappings, whereas disgust expressions showed the reverse pattern. Thus, memory was more accurate for the category assigned to approach in each group. This pattern persisted after accounting for face-recognition ability, rule-learning performance, and chance adjustment. Approach assignment also shifted evaluations of both categories in a positive direction and this evaluative effect extended to never-trained identities in Experiment 3. At the same time, more positive evaluations were not accompanied by a parallel change in rated arousal. These findings establish that learned category–action mappings shape expression-memory accuracy and evaluation, with evaluative consequences extending beyond trained identities.

papers.title: Adaptive Flexibility and Individual Stability in Audiovisual Cue Weighting under Different Listening Conditions
papers.authors: Chengjia Ye, James McQueen, Hans Rutger Bosker
papers.summary: Dutch listeners judged lexical stress while the researchers varied babble noise, looking at how they weighted pitch (f0), beat gestures, and lip movements. As noise got worse, people leaned less on pitch but didn't make up for it by leaning more on the visual cues, even though those stayed intact. Individual listeners' relative cue weighting stayed fairly stable across conditions, so there's flexibility at the group level and consistency within people.
papers.abstract: Phonological contrasts in speech are conveyed through multiple dimensions. Listeners may systematically adjust their cue weightings according to the context, such as under challenging listening conditions. However, individual listeners may also assign different perceptual weights to each dimension, giving rise to substantial individual differences. The present study examines how native listeners of Dutch weight an acoustic cue (fundamental frequency, f0) and two visual cues (beat gestures and lip movement) when perceiving lexical stress under different degrees of acoustic degradation induced by 16-talker babble noise. At the group level, f0 and beat gestures were robust cues to lexical stress, while the lip-movement effect was less consistent across conditions. Listeners systematically reduced their reliance on f0 as the noise became more severe, without a comparable increase in their reliance on either visual cue. At the individual level, listeners who relied more heavily on f0 in favorable listening conditions tended to show greater reductions in its absolute weighting under severe noise, with no evidence for a cross-condition trade-off between f0 and beat-gesture weighting; individual differences in relative cue weighting remained relatively stable across listening conditions. Taken together, these findings showcase both context-dependent adaptive flexibility and individual-specific stability in audiovisual cue weighting. More broadly, our findings suggest that dimension-selective attention principles may extend to cue-specific adjustments across sensory modalities under acoustic degradation. Specifically, down-weighting of a degraded acoustic cue does not necessarily entail compensatory up-weighting of visual cues, even though they remain physically intact.

papers.title: Developmental Differences in How Experiential and Observational Learning Shape Memory
papers.authors: Maria A. Woitow, Anthony I. Jang, Ben Eppinger et al.
papers.summary: Children (8–10) and adults (18–30) did a reinforcement learning task, either playing themselves or watching another player, with images shown incidentally so memory for them could be tested later. Both groups remembered images better after learning by doing than by watching, but adults' memory was boosted when someone gambled, especially after positive reward prediction errors. Children instead remembered images better when they rejected gambles, hinting that reward-related prediction signals shape memory differently across development.
papers.abstract: Children’s ability to learn and form memories through direct experience and observation increases with age. However, the development of the underlying mechanisms, particularly prediction errors (PEs), through which both learning modes influence memory, remains unclear. Using an incidental memory paradigm, we compared children (8–10 years) and adults (18–30 years) in how reward PEs (RPEs) during experiential and observational reinforcement learning affect episodic memory. Although children showed weaker learning performance, both age groups remembered images better after experiential than after observational learning, and they did not differ in recognition accuracy. However, adults showed greater memory strength and remembered images better when they or another player gambled for rewards, especially when associated with positive RPEs. In contrast, children recognized images better when they rejected gambles, and exploratory analyses linked better memory to larger unsigned RPEs when they accepted gambles. These findings suggest age differences in how one’s own and observed decisions, and potentially associated reward predictions, shape episodic memory.

papers.title: How does curriculum learning influence cognitive map formation?
papers.authors: Leonie Glitz, Zilu Liang, Helen Barron et al.
papers.summary: People learned one-step transitions on two maps, one taught in grouped row-and-column order and one in a spatially scattered order, and were then tested on multi-step navigation. Navigation was better after the scattered, disjoint curriculum. The suggestion is that grouped training fragments the mental map, while a more mixed order helps people integrate what they learned into a single map.
papers.abstract: Representing relational knowledge in a mental map is useful for adaptive behaviour. Here, we studied how curriculum learning (the use of different training regimes) influences the way that mental (or ‘cognitive’) maps are formed. We investigated how the order in which people learned one-step transitions impacted their subsequent ability to perform multi-step inference using the cognitive maps they had formed. Participants learned one map with a curriculum that grouped information by rows and columns (‘grouped curriculum’) and another that selected transitions for training in a spatially disjoint way (‘disjoint curriculum’). Subsequent multi-step navigation was performed better after training using the disjoint curriculum. We hypothesise that learning under a grouped curriculum results in mental fragmentation of the learned maps, which impairs subsequent navigation across rows and columns. By contrast, learning one-step transitions in a pseudo-random order facilitates subsequent integration of learned information into a mental map to enable adaptive behaviour.

papers.title: When Do Students Seek AI Help? Exploring Within-Person and Between-Person Differences
papers.authors: Richard Pak, Anne Collins McLaughlin, Ericka Rovira et al.
papers.summary: In a quiz where 398 undergrads chose on each of 30 trials to answer alone, consult an AI chatbot, or just rely on its answer, about half the variation in AI use reflected stable differences between students. The rest shifted from trial to trial, mostly tracking how knowledgeable students felt about the topic: they sought help when they felt less expert. The authors argue AI use looks more like adaptive help-seeking than a fixed trait, so helping students calibrate their own knowledge might work better than blanket rules.
papers.abstract: Objective: Research on student AI use typically asks who adopts these tools, treating use as a stable trait. Yet students face a fresh decision at every problem. We examined how much AI use reflects stable individual differences and how much varies within a student across tasks.Method: Undergraduates (N = 398) at two institutions completed 30 quiz trials, choosing on each trial to answer independently, consult an AI chatbot, or rely on an AI-generated answer. Students rated their topic expertise before each decision; cognitive abilities, AI attitudes, and demographics were also measured. Choices were analyzed with Bayesian multilevel multinomial logistic regression.Results: With moderately reliable AI, about half the variance in AI use reflected stable individual differences (intraclass correlations of 41% for chatbot use, 48% for full reliance); the remainder varied within individuals across trials. Self-assessed expertise accounted for this within-person variation: students sought help primarily when they felt unknowledgeable. Fluid intelligence predicted more chatbot consultation but less full delegation. Male students and those with more favorable AI attitudes delegated more readily.Conclusions: AI use is better described as adaptive help-seeking than as a fixed trait. Interventions targeting metacognitive calibration may prove more effective than blanket policies assuming uniform use.

papers.title: Adolescent development of decision making processes in working memory and links to pubertal timing and tempo
papers.authors: Erik Rimestad Frogner, Mads Lund Pedersen, Lars T. Westlye
papers.summary: Using longitudinal ABCD data from over 4,000 kids aged 9 to 17, researchers fit drift diffusion models to n-back working memory performance. Gains with age came mainly from more efficient information processing and faster non-decision processes, plus shifts in response caution and bias. Puberty added explanatory power beyond age: later pubertal timing and faster tempo went with better performance.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is associated with substantial improvements in cognitive performance, with faster and more accurate decisions, yet the underlying mechanisms and the role of pubertal maturation remain unclear. Pubertal maturation can be characterized by timing, capturing whether an individual reaches pubertal milestones before or after peers, and tempo, capturing how fast one progresses through puberty relative to peers. We applied computational modeling to examine developmental changes in decision making and working memory and tested whether pubertal timing and tempo explain variance beyond age. Using longitudinal data from 4201 participants (ages 9 – 17) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive DevelopmentSM (ABCD Study®), we characterized the development of accuracy, response times, and drift diffusion model parameters from an n-back task with generalized additive mixed models. Next, we compared age-only and puberty-informed models to test whether pubertal timing and tempo explain variance in cognitive development.We observed non-linear improvements in performance and all model parameters, with the largest changes in drift rate and non-decision time, indicating more efficient processing and faster non-decision processes. Additional non-linear changes in decision threshold, capturing the speed-accuracy tradeoff, and choice bias suggest strategic shifts in response caution and task strategy. Pubertal maturation explained additional individual differences beyond age, with later timing and faster tempo associated with better performance.This study shows that improvements in n-back performance are accompanied by increased information processing efficiency, faster non-decision processes, and adaptive decision policies, with pubertal timing and tempo contributing to heterogeneity in cognitive development.

papers.title: AX-CPT Measures Show Good Reliability and Shared Variance, but Raise Concerns About Their Validity
papers.authors: Niels Oliver Kempkens, Alodie Rey-Mermet
papers.summary: With 667 young adults doing the AX-CPT in five versions (letters, words, dot patterns, matrices, pictures), the researchers got good reliability for most indices and some shared variance across stimulus types. But the correlations didn't make sense theoretically. For instance, proactive and reactive control indices were very highly and positively correlated, which raises doubts about whether the task is measuring what it's supposed to.
papers.abstract: Attentional control refers to the ability to maintain a goal and goal-relevant information in the face of distraction. Previous research has highlighted the lack of reliability and shared variance in attentional-control measures. This may result from the heterogeneity of the control processes induced by the tasks. The aim of the present study was to reduce or control for this heterogeneity in two ways. First, we used one task – the AX-CPT – with different stimulus materials (letters, words, dot patterns, matrices, and pictures). In this task, a target response is required in trials where two specific stimuli occur in sequence (e.g., the letter “A” followed by the letter “X”). In all other trials, a non-target response is required. Second, we distinguished between proactive control (goal maintenance) and reactive control (goal reactivation) by computing separate indices for each process. Using data from 667 young adults, we obtained good reliability for most indices. Confirmatory factor analysis identified models with factors representing shared variance across stimulus materials. In a subsequent analysis, we bypassed the indices by modeling proactive and reactive control directly from error rates and response times. Using a bifactor modeling approach, we found shared variance across stimulus materials for error rates only. However, in both analyses, the pattern of latent correlations contradicted the expectations. For example, a positive and very high correlation was observed between indices representing proactive and reactive control. Overall, these findings raise concerns about the validity of AX-CPT measures.

papers.title: A Computational Model of Mental Rotation in Aphantasia
papers.authors: Shiu-Cheng Wang, Tomer David Ullman
papers.summary: Here's a computational model of mental rotation in aphantasia built on the 'broken rendering' idea: everyone identifies and rotates objects the same way, but only people with typical imagery can also render the rotated object into a pixel-like picture for a quick comparison. Both comparison sources feed one drift-diffusion process. Simulations matched the patterns in an earlier dataset, including slower but more accurate responses in aphantasia, which the authors take as support for broken rendering over 'different strategies' or 'lack of meta-access' accounts.
papers.abstract: People with aphantasia seem unable to create visual imagery, yet they perform mental manipulation of objects in the mind. Different frameworks have different views on how this is possible. Mental rotation is a particularly useful test case for comparing these frameworks, as people with aphantasia show systematic differences and similarities on this task compared to people without aphantasia. Here, we propose a computational model of mental rotation based on the ‘broken rendering’ account of aphantasia (Balaban &amp; Ullman, 2025), which separates physical/spatial representations from graphical, picture-like ones. Our model proposes that both people with and without aphantasia are similar in their identification and rotation of objects, but differ in the comparison stage: People with and without aphantasia can use spatial/physical similarity to compare rotated objects, but people with typical imagery can also render a rotated object back into a 2D, pixel-like representation, and carry out a fast-but-less-reliable comparison between such visual depictions. Both sources of comparison (physical and visual) provide evidence to a single drift-diffusion decision process. We used our model to generate simulated experimental data, which we compared to the detailed findings of Kay et al., 2024. We found that our model captures the qualitative and quantitative patterns of behavior in a mental rotation task for people with and without aphantasia, including the canonical increase in response time (and decrease in accuracy) with angle growth, the slower but more accurate responses in aphantasia, and the opposite within-group correlations. This lends support to the broader framework of ‘broken rendering’ over ‘different strategies’ and ‘lack of meta-access’ as approaches to aphantasia. The findings hold across a wide set of parameter settings, and the model makes novel and testable predictions for further study in mental rotation.

papers.title: On the Psychophysics of Morality: Moral choices obey Weber’s law
papers.authors: Ansgar D Endress, Peter Ayton
papers.summary: The idea here is that moral choices work like perception, with noise making judgments follow Weber's law. In the sacrifice-few-to-save-many scenarios, acceptability tracked the ratio of beneficiaries to victims rather than raw utility or harm. Large language models partly reproduced human behavior but mostly relied on different heuristics, favoring utility. The authors also say the model offers a parameter-free account of loss aversion.
papers.abstract: Moral decisions are often cast as conflicts between utilitarianism (maximizing good) and deontology (following rules). We propose a unitary psychophysical model where moral decisions operate like other perceptual systems, tracking the subjective (information-theoretic) certainty that outcomes achieve the greater good. Due to psychophysical noise, decisions follow Weber's law, with utilitarian and deontological responses as high- vs. low-uncertainty limit cases. Participants rated the acceptability of sacrificing fewer 'victims' to save more 'beneficiaries'. Acceptability tracked beneficiary:victim Weber ratios, but not utility or harm. Responses grew more utilitarian with decreased uncertainty, and more deontological with increased victim salience, but always tracked the beneficiary:victim ratio. Frontier large language models partially reproduced human behaviour, but most used different heuristics from humans, generally prioritizing utility over beneficiary:victim ratios. Beyond moral decisions, our model provides a mechanistic, parameter-free explanation of loss aversion. People thus seek the greater good, but do so under perceptual noise.

papers.title: Neural sensitivity to musical rhythm is associated with the temporal dynamics of statistical learning in speech
papers.authors: Claudia Iorio, Bahar Saadatmehr, Mohammadreza Edalati et al.
papers.summary: Adults heard structured and random artificial speech streams while EEG tracked syllable-rate and word-rate responses, and they also did rhythm tasks with music. Word-level tracking grew over exposure only in the structured stream, and people whose brains synchronized more strongly to musical rhythm showed different time courses of word extraction. This points to a shared mechanism for picking up temporal regularities in music and language.
papers.abstract: Statistical learning enables the extraction of structure from the environment, including word units from continuous speech. Yet inter-individual variability suggests contributions from other, potentially broader domain-general mechanisms. Here, we investigated whether individual differences in music rhythm processing are associated with the dynamics of statistical learning during speech segmentation, potentially reflecting shared sensitivity to temporal regularities across music and language. Adults were exposed to structured and random artificial speech streams while neural tracking at syllable and word rate frequencies was tracked over time using EEG to characterize the emergence of word representations. In addition, participants’ abilities to process rhythm in musical materials were assessed using behavioral and neural (EEG) measures. Neural measurements revealed robust tracking at the syllabic level in both structured and random streams, whereas word-level tracking emerged over exposure only in the structured stream condition. Importantly, individual differences in neural synchronization to musical rhythms were associated with the temporal dynamics of word extraction. These results suggest that individual differences in the ability to process temporal regularities in musical material are related to the efficiency with which statistical regularities are extracted from sequential language material. More broadly, the findings provide evidence for domain-general mechanisms supporting sensitivity to temporal structure regularities across auditory domains.

papers.title: Exploring Environmental Structure for Task-general Representation Learning
papers.authors: Haoxue Fan, Matt R. Nassar
papers.summary: This is a theoretical review arguing that people reuse abstract, task-general representations of structure shared across tasks, which are shaped by the sample of tasks they've experienced, over both short-term learning and development. Because people choose their own experiences using the representations they have, errors can become self-sustaining. The authors highlight directed and value-free random exploration as two strategies that correct different kinds of distortion.
papers.abstract: Humans are always facing new tasks, but they are not forced to solve them from scratch, sincethey are almost always able to leverage previous experience to scaffold current learning. Wepropose that what connects past to present is task-general representations: abstract knowledge ofthe structure shared across tasks that serves as a foundation for new learning. Treating tasksperformed in the past as samples from an unknown task distribution, we review how propertiesof the observed samples shape task general representations. We apply the same lens to twodifferent timescales; learning over the course of minutes to days and development over thecourse of months to years. We then consider how people exert control over their own taskdistributions. We propose that exploration, by diversifying experience, keeps task-generalrepresentations adaptive because people choose their experiences using the very representationsthey are learning, errors in those representations can become self-sustaining. Specifically, wehighlight directed and value-free random exploration as two distinct exploration strategies thatcorrect different distortions in task-general representation.

papers.title: Conflict, not category: What the pupil tracks in face pareidolia
papers.authors: Amanda K Robinson, Jing Liang, Blake William Saurels et al.
papers.summary: Forty participants viewed human faces, illusory faces in objects, and matched objects while pupil size was recorded. Faces and objects both caused constriction, but illusory faces caused dilation starting around 350 ms, even after controlling for luminance and emotional valence. The dilation was larger for stronger face percepts and didn't fade with repetition, suggesting the pupil reflects the conflict between seeing a face and seeing an object rather than the category itself.
papers.abstract: Illusory faces, the faces people see in inanimate objects, share the low-level image statistics of the objects they are made of while nonetheless being perceived as faces. Neural representations of illusory faces shift from face-like to object-like within roughly 200 ms, and observers explicitly categorise them as objects, yet the illusion remains compelling. We asked whether the pupil, a peripheral index of light and arousal, is sensitive to this dual identity. Forty participants viewed sequences of human faces, illusory faces in objects, and matched non-face objects while performing an orthogonal task at fixation. Human faces and objects both evoked pupil constriction, whereas illusory faces produced dilation beginning at approximately 350 ms. Thus, rather than resembling either category, illusory faces elicited a qualitatively different pupil response. This dissociation remained after controlling for luminance and emotional valence. Critically, within the illusory images the dilation scaled with the strength of the face percept, indexed by independent measures of face categorisation, and did not diminish across repetitions. These findings are consistent with the pupil tracking the conflict between the object and face interpretations, rather than stimulus category per se, revealing a physiological signature of the competing identities that define face pareidolia.

papers.title: Are psychedelic users less susceptible to visual illusions? Evidence from the Illusion Game
papers.authors: Dominique Makowski, Marco Sperduti, Oliver Collins et al.
papers.summary: In 118 adults, comparing people who had never used psychedelics, recent users, and past users, the researchers had them judge which of two targets was larger under visual illusions, and analyzed it with a drift diffusion model. Users set wider decision boundaries and made fewer errors, and an accuracy-independent illusion sensitivity index was about 22% lower in users. That fits the idea of relaxed priors, but since recent and past users looked alike, the authors are cautious about interpreting it.
papers.abstract: Classic psychedelics are thought to relax prior expectations, which should weaken visual illusions. Evidence is scarce, especially outside the acute state, and error rates, the usual measure of illusion sensitivity, also depend on overall performance. We tested 118 adults, of whom 44 had never used a classic psychedelic, 39 had used one within the last 30 days (the "afterglow" period) and 35 longer ago. They completed the Illusion Game, a response-time task of judging which of two targets is larger while the strength of an illusion (Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, vertical-horizontal) varies independently of the real difference between them. A hierarchical drift diffusion model was fitted to every choice and response time. Both user groups set wider decision boundaries than naïve participants, gathering more evidence before responding, and made fewer errors. We then computed an index of illusion sensitivity independent of overall accuracy: the effect of illusion strength on performance relative to that of the real difference. This index was 22% lower in users on average, equally in recent and past users, and unrelated to age, language, student status, psychological flexibility, distress or the intensity of the last experience. It correlated moderately across illusions, less than general performance did. Psychedelic users appeared somewhat less sensitive to illusions, as relaxed priors would predict, but the absence of a clear link with use recency limits interpretative confidence and generalizability.

papers.title: Developmental Cue Weighting in Turkish Sentence Comprehension: Morphosyntactic and Prosodic Sensitivity
papers.authors: Selim Tiryakiol, Leyla Zidani Eroğlu, Fatih Bayram
papers.summary: Turkish-speaking children (6–16) and adults listened to scrambled sentences in an eye-tracking study, to see how they use case marking and prosody. Accusative case marking helped both groups, and it showed up in eye movements soon after the relevant noun phrase, while prosody influenced only adults. Sensitivity to prosody grew with age while the benefit of case marking dipped slightly, consistent with cue-weighting models where reliable morphosyntactic cues are relied on first.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how monolingual Turkish children (n = 46, ages 6–16) and adults (n = 52, ages 19–57) use morphosyntactic (case marking) and prosodic cues during sentence comprehension, employing a visual world eye-tracking paradigm. Participants interpreted scrambled, verb-medial sentences across four experimental conditions: Neutral-Bare, Neutral-NP1accusative, Neutral-NP2accusative, and Prosody-Bare. Offline comprehension scores revealed that overt accusative case marking was a robust cue for both children and adults, while prosodic cues influenced only adults. Generalised linear mixed-effects models confirmed significant main effects of group and condition, and significant interactions (all p &lt; .001). Eye-tracking analyses showed that both groups used case marking in real time, with effects emerging shortly after the relevant noun phrase, while only adults demonstrated sensitivity to prosodic cues. Age-modelling revealed that sensitivity to prosodic cues increased with age (p &lt; .001), whereas the benefit of case marking decreased slightly. These findings support competition-based cue-weighting models, indicating that Turkish comprehenders first stabilise reliance on reliable morphosyntactic cues, with prosodic sensitivity emerging gradually through development and experience.
